message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a C++ URL parser library **purely as a black box**.

The only artifact is the compiled binary: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable
There is NO library source available anywhere on disk (do not go looking for url_parser.h/.cpp — it does not exist). Do not try to disassemble or run 'strings'. Use ONLY behavioral probing: run the binary with argument values and observe stdout.

Usage: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "<url>"
With fewer than 2 argv entries it returns exit code 1 and prints nothing.

It prints EXACTLY 18 lines, in this order (one per line, via std::cout << x << std::endl):
 1  scheme()          (string)
 2  authority()       (string)
 3  userinfo()        (string)
 4  host()            (string)
 5  port()            (int, prints -1 when absent)
 6  path()            (string)
 7  query()           (string)
 8  fragment()        (string)
 9  has_scheme()      (bool printed as 1/0)
10  has_authority()
11  has_userinfo()
12  has_host()
13  has_port()
14  has_path()
15  has_query()
16  has_fragment()
17  to_string()       (string)
18  is_valid()        (bool 1/0)

A labeled probe helper already exists at /tmp/probe.sh (takes any number of url args). If missing, recreate it:

  cat > /tmp/probe.sh << 'EOS'
  #!/bin/bash
  LABELS=(scheme authority userinfo host port path query fragment has_scheme has_authority has_userinfo has_host has_port has_path has_query has_fragment to_string is_valid)
  for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "=== INPUT: [$arg]"
    mapfile -t out < <(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$arg"; echo "EXIT:$?")
    for i in "${!LABELS[@]}"; do printf "  %-14s [%s]\n" "${LABELS[$i]}" "${out[$i]}"; done
  done
  EOS
  chmod +x /tmp/probe.sh

Note: /tmp/probe.sh renders empty fields as []. For inputs containing characters bash would mangle, invoke the binary directly with careful quoting, or use printf/hexdump to inspect raw bytes:
  /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$URL" | od -c | head -40

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verified; you may re-verify but do not spend most of your budget here):
- A scheme is recognized ONLY when the literal "://" appears. "mailto:user@example.com" yields NO scheme and the entire input becomes path. "//example.com/path" yields no scheme and the whole thing is path (authority is parsed only when "://" was found).
- scheme() is LOWERCASED ("HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM" -> scheme "http"), but host() case is preserved ("EXAMPLE.COM").
- authority() is RECONSTRUCTED from userinfo/host/port, not the raw substring: "http://example.com:80abc" -> authority "example.com:80"; "http://example.com:" -> authority "example.com".
- port parsing behaves like std::stoi + a range check: "80abc"->80, "+80"->80, " 80"->80, "065"->65, "0"->0, but "-80"->absent, "65536"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "abc"->absent, ""->absent. Absent port prints -1 with has_port 0 and is omitted from authority()/to_string().
- Splitting after authority: the FIRST '#' splits off fragment (so "#a#b" -> fragment "a#b"); then within the part BEFORE that '#', the FIRST '?' splits off query. "/p#a?b" -> fragment "a?b", no query.
- has_*() appear to be "field is non-empty" for strings ("http://example.com/#" -> fragment "" and has_fragment 0), and has_port() is port != -1. BUT has_authority() is NOT simply "authority string non-empty": "http://:8080" gives authority ":8080" yet has_authority 0 (host is empty there) — pin down the real rule.
- No path normalization ("/a/./b/../c" preserved), no percent-decoding ("%7E" preserved).
- is_valid(): "" -> 0, "http://" -> 0, "http://:8080" -> 0, but "example.com" -> 1, "/just/a/path" -> 1, "mailto:user@example.com" -> 1.

YOUR JOB: exhaustively probe your assigned family below. Run MANY probes (dozens — at least 40 distinct inputs; more is better). For every behavior you claim, you MUST have run the exact input. Derive precise, implementable rules (as if writing pseudocode), and explicitly flag anything ambiguous or surprising.

Return findings as structured output. Rules must be stated so a programmer can implement them without further probing. Include the concrete probe evidence (input -> the specific field values that matter) for each rule. Prefer many small precise rules over few vague ones.

YOUR ASSIGNED FAMILY:
IS_VALID() TRUTH TABLE — derive the exact predicate.
Known: "" -> 0, "http://" -> 0, "http://:8080" -> 0, "example.com" -> 1, "/just/a/path" -> 1, "mailto:user@example.com" -> 1.
Systematically probe to find the predicate. Hypotheses to discriminate: (a) valid iff input non-empty; (b) valid iff (scheme present => host non-empty) AND something non-empty; (c) valid iff host non-empty OR path non-empty; (d) something about scheme charset. Probe: "http://h" , "http://h/", "http://@h", "http://u@", "http://u@:80", "http:// " (space host), "http://?q", "http://#f", "http:///p" , "http:///", "?q=1", "#f", "?", "#", "/", " ", "  " (spaces only), "\t", "a", "://x", "://", "http://h:99999", "HTTP://H", "1abc://h", "a b://h". Also: does is_valid() depend on the scheme being a KNOWN scheme (http/https/ftp/etc.) — probe "zzz://h", "q://h", "x1://h". Does an empty path with a valid host stay valid? Does whitespace-only input count as non-empty (valid)? State the final predicate as exact pseudocode and give the full discriminating truth table.

B=/workspace/dataset/test18_executable
A=( h 8 ':' '/' '@' '#' )
bad=0;n=0
check(){ mapfile -t o < <("$B" "$1"); local pred=0; [[ -n "${o[3]}" || -n "${o[5]}" ]] && pred=1; ((n++)); [[ "$pred" != "${o[17]}" ]] && { ((bad++)); printf 'MM [%s] h=<%s> p=<%s> v=%s\n' "$1" "${o[3]}" "${o[5]}" "${o[17]}"; }; }
for a in "${A[@]}"; do for b in "${A[@]}"; do for c in "${A[@]}"; do for d in "${A[@]}"; do check "$a$b$c$d"; done; done; done; done
echo "exh2 tested=$n mismatches=$bad"
EOS
chmod +x /tmp/exh2.sh; /tmp/exh2.sh
echo "--- scheme-identity test (host present vs absent)"
for sc in http https ftp file ws mailto data zzz q x1 HTTP Http "a-b" "a+b" "a.b" "1" "9z" "" " " "%" "://"; do
  a=$(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "${sc}://h" | sed -n '1p;18p' | tr '\n' ' ')
  b=$(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "${sc}://" | sed -n '1p;18p' | tr '\n' ' ')
  printf "scheme[%-6s] with-host: scheme=<%s> | no-host: scheme=<%s>\n" "$sc" "$a" "$b"
done

content.text: Exhaustive verification complete: 4,097 exhaustively-enumerated inputs plus ~6,000 fuzz/hand probes, zero mismatches against a single predicate.

rules.rule: THE PREDICATE: is_valid() == ( !host().empty() || !path().empty() ). Equivalently: is_valid() == (has_host() || has_path()). Nothing else in the parse result influences it. Pseudocode: bool is_valid() const { return !host_.empty() || !path_.empty(); }

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of scheme presence. 'http:///p' -> scheme 'http', host '', path '/p' -> valid 1. '/just/a/path' -> no scheme, path non-empty -> valid 1. 'http://' -> scheme 'http', host '', path '' -> valid 0. There is no 'scheme implies host' requirement.

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of the scheme's identity and charset — there is NO known-scheme whitelist. With a non-empty host all of these are valid 1: http, https, ftp, file, ws, mailto, data, 'zzz', 'q', 'x1', 'HTTP', 'Http', 'a-b', 'a+b', 'a.b', '1', '9z', '1abc', 'a b' (with a space), '%' , ' ' (scheme is literally one space). With an empty host and empty path all of the same schemes give valid 0. Scheme charset/length/case is never validated.
is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of query(). 'http://:80?q' -> host '', path '', query 'q' -> valid 0. '?a=b' -> query 'a=b' -> valid 0. A non-empty query can never rescue an otherwise-invalid URL.
is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of fragment(). '#f' -> fragment 'f' -> valid 0. 'http://:80#f' -> fragment 'f', host '', path '' -> valid 0. 'http://u@#f' -> userinfo 'u', fragment 'f' -> valid 0.

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of userinfo(). 'http://u@' -> userinfo 'u', host '', path '' -> valid 0. 'http://u:p@' -> valid 0. 'http://u@/p' -> userinfo 'u', host '', path '/p' -> valid 1 (the path, not the userinfo, makes it valid).

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of port(). 'http://:8080' -> port 8080, host '', path '' -> valid 0. 'http://:80/p' -> port 80, host '', path '/p' -> valid 1. 'http://h:65536' and 'http://h:99999' and 'http://h:-1' -> port absent (-1) but host 'h' -> valid 1. An out-of-range/unparseable port never invalidates.

is_valid() is INDEPENDENT of to_string(). Counterexamples both ways: '://x' -> to_string '' (empty!) yet valid 1; '?a=b' -> to_string '?a=b' (non-empty) yet valid 0; 'http://u@' -> to_string 'http://u@' yet valid 0. Do not implement is_valid via to_string.

Whitespace and control bytes count as ordinary non-empty content. ' ' (one space) -> path ' ' -> valid 1. '  ' -> valid 1. tab -> path tab -> valid 1. 'a\nb' -> path 'a', query 'b' -> valid 1. 0x01 -> path 0x01 -> valid 1. 'http:// ' -> host ' ' (a single space), has_host 1 -> valid 1. 'http://  ' -> host '  ' -> valid 1. There is NO trimming and no whitespace rejection.
Empty input is the only length-0 case: '' -> all fields empty -> valid 0.

Inputs that reduce to pure delimiters with no host and no path are invalid: '?' -> 0, '#' -> 0, '??' -> 0, '?#' -> 0, '#?' -> 0, '###' -> 0, '??q' -> 0, '://' -> 0, '://:80' -> 0, '://u@' -> 0, 'http://?' -> 0, 'http://#' -> 0, 'http://?#' -> 0, 'ZZZ://' -> 0. In every one of these both host and path are empty.

Any single character other than '?' and '#' is valid, because it lands in path: 'a' -> 1, '0' -> 1, '-' -> 1, '.' -> 1, '/' -> 1, ':' -> path ':' -> 1, '%' -> 1, ' ' -> 1, tab -> 1. Only '?' and '#' are consumed as delimiters and leave path empty.

When '://' is present the authority is parsed even if the scheme part is EMPTY, and that parsed host makes the URL valid with has_scheme 0: '://x' -> scheme '' (has_scheme 0), host 'x', valid 1. '://h:80' -> host 'h', valid 1. ' ://h' -> scheme ' ' (has_scheme 1), host 'h', valid 1.

has_authority() == !host().empty() — it matched exactly in all ~7000 probes, including 'http://:8080' (authority ':8080', has_authority 0), 'http://u@' (authority 'u@', has_authority 0), and 'http:// ' (host ' ', has_authority 1). So has_authority() is exactly has_host().
is_valid() never depends on input length or byte values: a 300-char host -> 1; a 200-char all-'/' path -> 1; non-UTF8 bytes 0xFF 0xFE as path -> 1; 'café' as path or host -> 1.

Process behavior: with argc >= 2 the binary always prints exactly 18 lines and exits 0, including for invalid URLs ('' , '?' -> exit 0). With argc < 2 it prints nothing and exits 1. is_valid being 0 does NOT change the exit code or suppress output.

evidence.note: scheme present but host and path empty -> 0
port present does not make it valid; has_authority 0 despite authority ':8080'
userinfo present does not make it valid
query present does not make it valid
fragment present does not make it valid
to_string non-empty but valid 0 -> kills the to_string hypothesis
scheme present + empty host + non-empty path -> 1; kills 'scheme implies host required'
single space becomes path ' ' -> has_path 1 -> valid 1 (no trimming)
host is a single space -> has_host 1 -> valid 1
empty scheme (has_scheme 0) but authority still parsed; to_string is EMPTY yet valid 1 -> kills to_string hypothesis in the other direction
scheme with a space is accepted; scheme charset is never validated
out-of-range port silently dropped, still valid because host non-empty
host empty + port 80 + path '/p' -> valid 1 via path alone

ambiguities: `has_host() || has_path()` and `has_authority() || has_path()` are OBSERVATIONALLY IDENTICAL: has_authority() == !host().empty() in every one of ~7000 probes (I fuzz-checked this equality explicitly: 0 divergences). I could not construct any input where authority-presence and host-non-emptiness differ, so which one is_valid() internally consults is undeterminable. Implementing either gives byte-identical output.
Likewise `!path_.empty()` vs `has_path()` cannot be distinguished, since has_path() == !path().empty() held on all probes (including path ' ', path tab, path 0x01).
Whether is_valid() is a stored flag computed at parse time or recomputed on each call is unobservable from a single-shot CLI (each run parses once).

Surprising (outside my family but load-bearing for anyone reimplementing): to_string() for '://x' is the EMPTY string even though host is 'x' and is_valid is 1; and to_string() for '://h/p?q#f' is '/p?q#f' — the authority is dropped from to_string when has_scheme is false. This is why is_valid must NOT be derived from to_string.

I found no input at all where the predicate fails. If a counterexample exists it must live outside: all strings of length <=4 over {a,:,/,?,#,@,space}, all strings of length 4 over {h,8,:,/,@,#}, 6000 random token-concatenations over a 33-token alphabet, and ~180 hand-chosen probes (long strings, non-UTF8 bytes, control chars, embedded newline, IPv6-ish brackets, percent-encodings).
